units.title: 3.1 Component 1: Philosophy of religion and ethics

subtopics.title: Arguments for the existence of God

outcomes.text: Explain the design, ontological and cosmological arguments of Paley, Anselm and Aquinas, with criticisms from Hume, Gaunilo, Kant and Russell.
Judge the arguments' basis in observation or thought, strengths, weaknesses, status as proofs, and value for faith.
Explain natural and moral evil and the logical and evidential problems of evil.
Compare Hick's soul-making theodicy, the free will defence and Griffin's process theodicy, with strengths and weaknesses.
Distinguish visions, numinous experience (Otto) and mystical experience (James, Stace).
Evaluate challenges to verifying experiences, including science, religious replies and Swinburne's principles of credulity and testimony.
Assess the influence of religious experience and its value for faith.
Compare cognitive and non-cognitive views of religious language and the verification and falsification challenges.
Explain responses from Hick, Hare's blik and Wittgenstein's language games.
Explain symbolic (Tillich), analogical (Aquinas) and Via Negativa views and evaluate them.
Compare understandings of miracle: realist and anti-realist, violation of natural law or natural event.
Compare Hume and Wiles on miracles and their significance for religion.
Explain the soul, Descartes' argument for it, and the body/soul relationship.
Discuss the possibility of continuing personal existence after death.
Explain natural moral law, double effect and proportionalism (Aquinas), situation ethics (Fletcher) and virtue ethics (Aristotle).
Compare how each theory approaches moral decisions, applying them to theft and lying, and assess strengths and weaknesses.

subtopics.title: Applied ethics: human life and death

outcomes.text: Apply natural moral law, situation ethics and virtue ethics to embryo research, cloning and designer babies.
Apply them to abortion, voluntary euthanasia, assisted suicide and capital punishment.
Apply the theories to animals as food, intensive farming, scientific procedures, blood sports and animal organ transplants.
Explain Divine Command Theory, utilitarian naturalism and intuitionist non-naturalism, and evaluate them.
Explain conditions of moral responsibility: free will and knowing right from wrong.
Compare libertarianism, hard determinism and compatibilism, and link responsibility to reward and punishment.
Compare religious and non-religious ideas about conscience and its role in lying, promises and adultery, and its value as a guide.
Compare Bentham and Kant on moral decisions and judge their fit with religious moral decision making.

units.title: 3.2 Component 2: Study of religion and dialogues

outcomes.text: Study Buddhism beliefs, teachings, values and practices, how texts are interpreted, and differences within the faith.
Recognise the technical terms Dukkha, Anicca, Nirvana, karma and ahimsa.

subtopics.title: Buddhism: sources of wisdom and authority

outcomes.text: Explain the Buddha's significance for Theravada and Mahayana, including skilful means and the burning house parable.
Explain Dukkha and the debate on whether Buddhism is pessimistic.
Explain the nature, authority and use of the Pali Canon and debates over its accuracy.
Compare Theravada and Mahayana concepts of Buddha and the Trikaya doctrine.
Explain Anicca and the Mahayana doctrine of emptiness.
Explain Nirvana, its indescribability and the 80th dilemma of King Milinda.
Explain the goals of better rebirth and Nirvana, and the arhat and bodhisattva ideals.
Explain anatta, the five aggregates and the chariot analogy.
Explain samsara, karma, realms of becoming, and the Dalai Lama as Avalokitesvara.

subtopics.title: Buddhism: good conduct and moral principles

outcomes.text: Explain moral conduct, intention, kusala and akusala, free will and moral responsibility.
Explain the five precepts and the Mahayana six perfections.
Apply ahimsa to the embryo, animals and war, with differing Buddhist views.
Explain the Thai Sangha, its lay relationship, 21st century role and Wat Phra Dhammakaya.
Compare Theravada and Mahayana devotion, Buddha images and merit.
Explain meditation on the eightfold path and its use as therapy.
Explain historical and social influences on Buddhist views in Thailand.
Discuss the revival of the nuns' order, Dhammananda, Sakyadhita, and views on celibacy, marriage and same sex relationships.
Explain how science has influenced Buddhism, challenges to karma and miracles, and responses.
Discuss the value of science, quantum physics, Thich Nhat Hanh and the Dalai Lama, and genetic engineering.
Explain secularisation challenges in Britain and Buddhist responses to materialism.
Discuss Amaravati, Triratna, Secular Buddhism and Engaged Buddhism.
Compare Batchelor and Brazier on the nature of Buddhism.
Explain Buddhism's development in Britain and diversity within it.
Discuss whether Buddhism is a collection of traditions, Ashoka's Edict 12, and Nichiren views.
Discuss Buddhist responses to religious freedom.
Examine how developments in belief influenced and were influenced by philosophy of religion: reasonableness, meaning, coherence and 'belief in' versus 'belief that'.
Analyse the religion's teaching on its God or ultimate reality, self and afterlife, authority, religious experience, science, other faiths' truth claims and miracles.
Explain responses to deontological (Kant), teleological (Bentham) and virtue ethics, and how far the religion's ethics fits each.
Explain responses to life and death issues, theft and lying, marriage, same sex relationships, transgender matters, genetic engineering, wealth, tolerance and religious freedom.
Explain views on free will, moral responsibility and conscience, and assess how other ethical perspectives challenge or support the religion's views.
Study Christianity beliefs, teachings, values and practices, how texts are interpreted, and differences within the faith.
Know that exam terms are translated except for names of people, texts and schools.

subtopics.title: Christianity: sources of wisdom and authority

outcomes.text: Compare Christian views of the Bible's nature and authority.
Compare Protestant and Catholic views on Bible and Church authority.
Compare views of Jesus' authority, using the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:38-48).
Explain monotheism, the Trinity and Jesus as Son of God (John 10:30; 1 Corinthians 8:6).
Discuss God as personal, Father and Love, anthropomorphic language and Christian feminist views.
Explain God in process theology.
Explain the purposes of life: glorify God, prepare for judgement, build God's kingdom.
Explain resurrection of the flesh (Augustine), spiritual resurrection and 1 Corinthians 15.
Compare interpretations of judgement, heaven, hell, purgatory and objective immortality.

subtopics.title: Christianity: good conduct and moral principles

outcomes.text: Explain justification by works, by faith and predestination.
Compare views of sanctity of life on the embryo and the just war theory with weapons of mass destruction.
Explain dominion and stewardship over animals and the environment.
Compare Catholic and Baptist views of infant baptism.
Compare Catholic and Baptist Holy Communion and Luke 22:17-20.
Trace developments in the Church's idea of mission since the early 20th century.
Explain influences: Biblical criticism, 1 Timothy 2:8-15, changing gender roles and women's rights.
Discuss female ordination in the Church of England and Hampson and Ruether on patriarchy.
Compare views on celibacy, marriage, same sex relationships and transgender matters.
Explain the God of the gaps, responses to Darwin and the Big Bang, and creationism.
Explain Polkinghorne's view of compatibility and responses to genetic engineering.
Explain responses to materialism and McGrath's The Dawkins Delusion defence.
Discuss Fresh Expressions, the House Church movement and liberationist approaches.
Compare exclusivism (John 14:6), inclusivism (anonymous Christians) and how denominations view each other.
Explain Hick's pluralism and its implications, and Christian views on religious freedom.
Examine how developments in belief influenced and were influenced by philosophy of religion: reasonableness, meaning, coherence and 'belief in' versus 'belief that'.

Study Hinduism beliefs, teachings, values and practices, how texts are interpreted, and differences within the faith.
Recognise the technical terms Trimurti, avatar, karma, ahimsa and darshan.

subtopics.title: Hinduism: sources of wisdom and authority

outcomes.text: Explain shruti, the Vedas, Upanishads and the Purusha Sukta on caste.
Explain smrti texts: Ramayana, Bhagavad Gita and Manusmrti.
Explain the role of gurus today, including Swami Sivananda.
Discuss ideas about God and gods in the Rig Veda.
Explain the Trimurti, Brahman and avatars, especially Krishna and Rama.
Explain Nirguna and Saguna Brahman and Kena Upanishad 1:3-8.
Explain the four aims of life and understandings of moksha.
Explain atman, Advaita Vedanta, Samkhya and the chariot parable (Katha Upanishad 3).
Explain samsara, reincarnation, types of karma and the realms of reincarnation.

subtopics.title: Hinduism: good conduct and moral principles

outcomes.text: Explain good conduct through karma and karma yoga.
Explain Sanatana dharma and Varnashrama dharma.
Apply ahimsa to the embryo, animals and war, including Gandhi's non-violence.
Explain the paths of Yoga and their suitability for different characters.
Explain bhakti yoga, darshan, pilgrimage to the Ganges and puja.
Explain the changing role of ashrams, including Sivananda and Skanda Vale.
Explain western influence, changing gender roles and women's rights in India.
Discuss Ram Mohan Roy, Manushi, and views on celibacy, marriage, divorce, same sex relationships and transgender matters.
Explain Hindu responses to Darwin and the Big Bang, including ISKCON.
Explain Radhakrishnan's view and Vedas as revealing science, and responses to genetic engineering.
Compare Ram Mohan Roy and Dayananda Saraswati, and explain Vivekananda's Practical Vedanta and the Ramakrishna Mission.
Explain British secularisation challenges, Brahmo Samaj UK and ISKCON.
Explain Vedanta as religion, the importance of India and sacred sites abroad.
Discuss religious freedom, Hindutva, personal law and the Sangh Parivar.

Study Islam beliefs, teachings, values and practices, how texts are interpreted, and differences within the faith.
Recognise the technical terms Tawhid, Barzakh, Al-Qadr and Jihad.

subtopics.title: Islam: sources of wisdom and authority

outcomes.text: Explain the Qur'an's nature, revelation, compilation, Arabic text, and translation as interpretation.
Explain Muhammad as Khatam an-Nabiyyin and views on hadiths.
Explain the authority of Imams in Shi'a Islam.
Explain Tawhid and the Throne verse (2:255).
Explain God's names, anthropomorphic descriptions and Ashari, Hanbali and Mutazili views.
Explain Sufi ideas of God, emanation and the verse of Light (24:35).
Explain life as worship and a moral test, preparing for the afterlife.
Compare views of Al-Qadr: Mutazili, Ashari and Shi'a Bada.
Explain Akhirah, Barzakh, judgement, heaven and hell, including 47:15.

Explain sanctity of life, embryo, lesser jihad, weapons of mass destruction and terrorism.
Explain Khalifah stewardship of environment and animals.
Compare Shi'a and Sunni views of being a Muslim.
Explain the five pillars, Salah differences, Jummah prayer and modern Hajj.
Explain the mosque's changing role, including the London Central Mosque.

Explain Muslim migration to the UK since the 1950s and diversity in Britain.

outcomes.text: Compare views of the Tenakh as absolute Word of God or inspired by God and its use.
Compare views of the Babylonian Talmud's nature and authority.
Explain the role and authority of rabbis and the Beth Din.
Explain monotheism and Maimonides' Thirteen Principles.
Discuss God as personal, King and Father, and Genesis 3:8.
Explain Buber's God as Eternal Thou.
Explain purposes of life: obedience, bringing the Messiah, repairing the world.
Explain She'ol, the soul, resurrection, immortality, the Pittsburgh Platform and God's justice.
Explain reincarnation in kabbalistic thinking.
